> Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection).

The requirement provides a false sense of security. It suggests a simple one solution ("encoding or escaping") for a highly complex, context-dependent problem. 
* “**dynamically building JavaScript Contnet**” is ambiguous, there are many different contexts in JavaScript each requires different type of encoding, escaping or none at all. If needed I can share the real-world examples.
* Misleads developers into skipping serialization, example : let json = '{"name": "' + userInput + '"}'; JSON is a data format , if we use JSON.stringfy or returning via api, escaping is not needed.
* The requirement groups JavaScript and JSON together, potentially implying they are equally dangerous, which may confuse developers about their distinct risk profiles (JavaScript’s executable nature vs. JSON’s data-only nature).
* The statement oversimplifies a complex, context-dependent problem by suggesting "encoding or escaping" as a one solution, potentially leading developers to overlook context-specific measures like sanitization, validation, or avoiding unsafe APIs.

This requires to improve clarity and accuracy which prevents oversimplified mental model of security that is likely to lead a well-intentioned developer to write vulnerable code.

> JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight data-interchange format. It is easy for humans to read and write. It is easy for machines to parse and generate. **It is based on a subset of the JavaScript Programming Language** Standard ECMA-262 3rd Edition

We talk about building dynamically a document, we talk about syntax, and JSON uses JavaScript syntax.

Your comments are in context when you are using the JSON, not when you are building it. But I already described it all in https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3212#issuecomment-3109561454.

The concern here is two fold:
1) When it comes to webpages is, if you try to display a piece of JSON without encoding it properly in a web page, it could lead to code execution/XSS. A common anti-pattern is to embed JSON in a webpage with stringify, which leads to XSS. 
2) Another problem is parsing JSON server-side in Node.js with eval or similar - this will lead to code execution. So while JSON is not technically JavaScript - JSON does require very special handling so it will not be executed as code.

PS: JSON originated from JavaScript but is now a completely independent, language-neutral data format. > Could you please clarify Why does 1.2.3 emphasize ‘escaping and encoding’ but not serialization via JSON.stringify, a safer standard for JSON construction

When you want to add a piece of JSON to a JS UI, like when you are rendering a React page, it’s a common performance pattern to embed the initial JSON in the template as opposed to XHR/Fetch. Just on the first hit.

In this situation, JSON.stringify is actually *dangerous* and can lead to XSS/Web page injection. It’s safer to embed JSON on web pages using JS encoding/escaping.

If you would like I can give you an example that shows *why* JSON.stringify in a webpage is actually dangerous! 🙏🏼

My original question focused on why **serialization** (using JSON.stringify) is not mentioned in the requirement, when encoding and escaping being mentioned. I advocate that serialization is essential for **safe JSON construction**.

The “common performance pattern” used in SSR frameworks. Every major server-side rendering framework (like Next.js, Nuxt, etc.) follows this safe pattern:

* **Use JSON.stringify() on the server to serialize data,**
* **Then apply context-specific escaping (e.g., for <script> or HTML).** 

Here's an example from Next.js, where they serialize the data with JSON.stringify() and then escape the result to safely embed it in the HTML page.

So as per me:

* **Serialization (JSON.stringify) is essential for [JSON construction](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/server/render.tsx#L1237)**.
* **Escaping and encoding is required for safe embedding, particularly into script or HTML contexts.Please [refer the specs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/e2b6a50aec59c42b2c0450a899005d5dbd5cb932/test/unit/htmlescape.test.ts#L4)**

PS: Serialization and encoding are related.

* Serialization preserves structure (objects in memory ↔ bytes).
* Encoding preserves representation (bytes ↔ different bytes/text).

They’re complementary and commonly stacked. Think: serialize first, then encode as needed for transport or storage.

Before further discussion, I would like to know, do you wish to correct the below statement/thinking or still on the same note that "No one should build JSON that way" https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3212#issuecomment-3153087277.

> There is no good reason why someone should build JSON using string concat.

Manual JSON creation with string building is very performance friendly, especially in the world of Java or C++ which have specific memory issues. It’s frequently used for webscale applications or when building very large JSON.  Many of these JSON libraries take a lot of memory to hold JSON state. That’s not needed for string concatenated JSON.

It’s not something I do often, but I have used it recently when building a C++ piece of middleware for a very high volume log system. The difference was dramatic in a positive way when we moved to string concatenated JSON.
